findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that `interprocess_lock` and the janitor GC guard call `release_exclusive` only after a successful `take_*` (the `locked`-flag shape of `fsutil.sibling_exclusive_lock`), and that the contended-GC path returns `skipped="locked"` without calling release.
evidence: janitor.py:344-354: `try: fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) except OSError: return GcResult(skipped="locked") ... finally: fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)`: the unlock runs even when the lock was never taken.

lock_kernel.py:153-154: on Windows, release_exclusive is `msvcrt.locking(fd, msvcrt.LK_UNLCK, 1)`, which errors when the range is not locked by this handle (POSIX LOCK_UN on an unheld flock is a silent no-op).
fsutil.py:53-61: `sibling_exclusive_lock` already guards against this with `locked = False ... if locked: release_exclusive(fd)`.
The plan's failure-path test is POSIX-only ('Failure path: ... (existing janitor test)' under the POSIX bullet), so the Windows-only divergence cannot be caught before the 3 sweep runs.
findings.finding: The plan does not say that the lock is released only after it was actually acquired. Both `run_gc` (janitor.py:342-354) and `interprocess_lock` (git_fetch.py:67-77) currently release unconditionally in `finally`. If the implementer swaps `fcntl.flock(LOCK_UN)` for `lock_kernel.release_exclusive` in that same shape, the Windows leg calls `msvcrt.locking(fd, LK_UNLCK, 1)` on a byte this handle never locked, and that raises OSError. In `run_gc`, the error raised from `finally` replaces the `return GcResult(skipped="locked")`, so a contended GC pass raises instead of skipping. In `interprocess_lock`, a failed acquire gets masked by a second error from the release.
findings.location: Approach › Locks (interprocess_lock / janitor GC guard); Testing › 'Failure path: a held GC guard still yields GcResult(skipped="locked")'
scenarios: Two GC passes overlap on Windows (the resident janitor plus a detached gc_trigger worker). The loser's take_exclusive raises EACCES, the `finally` unlock raises, and run_gc raises instead of returning skipped="locked". gc_trigger then logs 'snapshot-GC pass failed'.
interprocess_lock's take_blocking_exclusive raises a non-contention OSError (e.g. EBADF). The unconditional release raises a second error that replaces the original.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Locks bullet, add: "Release mirrors `fsutil.sibling_exclusive_lock`: set `locked = True` only after `take_blocking_exclusive`/`take_exclusive` returns, and in `finally` call `release_exclusive(fd)` only `if locked`, then `os.close(fd)`. In run_gc, the contention path (`is_contention(exc)`) returns `GcResult(skipped="locked")` without attempting a release." Optionally implement `interprocess_lock` by delegating to `sibling_exclusive_lock(lock_path, lock_name=lock_path.name)`, so the guarded shape is reused instead of copied.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the janitor GC guard, call `release_exclusive` only when `take_exclusive` succeeded (track a `locked` flag like `sibling_exclusive_lock` does), and re-raise non-contention OSErrors (`not is_contention(exc)`) instead of reporting them as `skipped="locked"`.
evidence: janitor.py:345-354: `try: fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) except OSError: return GcResult(skipped="locked")` ... `finally: fcntl.flock(fd, fcntl.LOCK_UN)` runs even when the lock was never taken
lock_kernel.py:152-154: the Windows release is `msvcrt.locking(fd, msvcrt.LK_UNLCK, ...)`, with no guard for a lock that isn't held
Plan: "The janitor's non-blocking GC guard uses `lock_kernel.take_exclusive` and `is_contention`", with no release shape stated
The plan's failure-path test ("a held GC guard still yields `GcResult(skipped=\"locked\")`") runs only on POSIX, where unlocking an unheld flock is a no-op, so it can't catch this
Evidence class: Partially-verified (lock_kernel's Windows release surface was inspected; the unlock-of-unheld-range error behaviour can't be probed from this host)
findings.finding: The plan says to move the janitor GC guard to `take_exclusive`/`is_contention` but doesn't say how the lock is released. Today the `finally` unlocks unconditionally, even when the lock was refused. On the Windows leg, `release_exclusive` calls `msvcrt.locking(fd, LK_UNLCK, 1)`, which normally raises an error when the handle doesn't hold the range. A direct swap would make the contended path raise instead of returning `GcResult(skipped="locked")`, exactly on the platform this ticket targets.
scenarios: Two GC passes overlap on Windows: the second's take_exclusive fails with EACCES, the code returns skipped=locked, and then the finally block's release_exclusive raises OSError, which replaces the return value
findings.suggested_fix: Mirror fsutil.sibling_exclusive_lock: open the fd, set `locked=False`, try `take_exclusive(fd)` and set `locked=True`. On an OSError where `is_contention(exc)` is true, return `GcResult(skipped="locked")`; otherwise re-raise. Then run `_gc_pass`. In `finally`, call `release_exclusive(fd)` only if `locked`, and always call `os.close(fd)`.

findings.finding: The plan has interprocess_lock open its own fd and call take_blocking_exclusive/release_exclusive directly. That rebuilds rebar._store.fsutil.sibling_exclusive_lock, which already does exactly that: makedirs the parent, os.open O_CREAT|O_RDWR, take_blocking_exclusive, then release_exclusive and close in finally. The plan uses that same helper for alert_store in the same bullet. Leaving a second hand-rolled copy of the open/lock/release/close sequence in git_fetch.py keeps two copies of the lock lifecycle to maintain.

Testing relies on "a held GC guard still yields GcResult(skipped="locked") (existing janitor test)". If that test holds the guard in the same process and lock_kernel uses per-process record locks, the guard silently stops contending.
findings.finding: The plan swaps three POSIX fcntl lock sites onto lock_kernel/sibling_exclusive_lock without stating that lock_kernel's POSIX leg keeps each site's current exclusion semantics. Two differences matter. (a) If the current code uses flock (per open file description) and lock_kernel uses fcntl/lockf record locks (per process), two threads or two handles in one process stop excluding each other. (b) alert_store's lock target may move from the data file to a sibling `.append.lock`, so an old-version and a new-version process appending concurrently would no longer exclude each other.
scenarios: A threaded caller of interprocess_lock in one process: both threads acquire at once under per-process lockf semantics, and the git fetch runs concurrently.
An existing in-process janitor contention test stops seeing contention on Linux.
During an upgrade, an old process locks the alert day file while a new process locks .append.lock, and appends interleave.

findings.finding: The plan alters several failure arms without stating what each caller ends up seeing. (1) It removes the mkdir spin fallback in interprocess_lock. On a host where no kernel leg applies, lock_kernel now raises NoExclusiveLegError, but the plan does not say whether that is fatal or permanent for the fetch caller, nor that it is surfaced rather than caught. (2) The janitor guard maps is_contention to skipped="locked", but a non-contention OSError from take_exclusive has no stated disposition: propagate, or skip? (3) The plan does not state what surfaces on Windows if take_blocking_exclusive cannot acquire: msvcrt LK_LOCK gives up after its retry window and raises OSError. Is that retried or fatal?
scenarios: A snapshot fetch on a host without a kernel leg now raises where it previously spun.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either serialize `alert_store.patch_bug_filed`'s read-modify-replace under the same sibling lock as `append` (name it for the file, not for 'append'), or state explicitly that the patch-vs-append race is out of scope and why.
evidence: alert_store.py:126-151: `for jf in sorted(store_dir.glob("*.jsonl"), reverse=True): ... jf.read_text(...) ... _atomic_write(jf, ...)` takes no lock.
alert_store.py:153: `except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 — skip an unwritable/unparseable alert file` hides a Windows replace failure.
The lock name chosen by the plan, '.append.lock', limits it to appends by design.
findings.finding: The new alert-store lock covers only `append`. `patch_bug_filed` in the same module rewrites the same daily `*.jsonl` file with read_text, rewrite and `fsutil.atomic_write` (os.replace), outside any lock. A concurrent append that lands between its read and its replace is silently lost, on POSIX and on Windows. On Windows, os.replace onto a file that an appender has open fails with PermissionError, and the per-file `except Exception: continue` swallows it, so the bug_ticket_id patch is silently dropped. The plan adds a portable lock for this file without making it cover every writer of the file.
scenarios: A reconciler appends an alert while another instance runs patch_bug_filed on today's file. The appended line is overwritten by the rewrite (POSIX), or the patch fails silently (Windows), so the alert later re-files a duplicate bug because bug_ticket_id was never recorded.
findings.suggested_fix: Use one directory-level lock, e.g. `sibling_exclusive_lock(today, lock_name=".alerts.lock")`, in both `append` and the per-file rewrite in `patch_bug_filed` (take it around the read_text…_atomic_write of each candidate file). The dotfile name still keeps the lock out of retention and out of the `*.jsonl` globs.
